answer.rationale: The mandate is an 18% unit-cost cut on a 14-day runway with the line at 94% utilization and zero buffer. Switching primary (memory c2) or adding a second source (memory c3) would jeopardize delivery continuity during the first cycle, which conflicts with the no-extra-delivery-risk constraint and with the stable two-cycle integration implied by c1. Deferring (c5) cannot satisfy the 14-day cliff because the contract does not auto-renew, so inaction is not an option here. Renegotiating with the incumbent at renewal is the path supported by c4 (benchmarking recovered real margin on price and terms last cycle) and c6 (multi-year terms lowered unit cost without reducing service scope). At 94% utilization, the incumbent's existing integration and delivery cadence are the supply reliability asset, so I want to use that position at the bargaining table rather than risk a swap. Pulling c2 and c6 for verification before committing: c2 confirms the incumbent's invoicing accuracy and onboarding speed if I needed to switch, and c6 confirms the incumbent's willingness to extend volume pricing for term, which is exactly the lever I plan to pull. The intended action is negotiate_terms, structured as a short guarded test rather than a large irreversible commitment. The primary lever is a multi-year commitment in exchange for the 18% unit-cost reduction (drawing on c6's volume-pricing pattern and c4's benchmarking leverage). If the incumbent will not move enough on unit cost, the fallback lever is improved payment terms and service scope held flat, not a vendor change in this cycle. This preserves delivery continuity, protects the 94% utilization line, and uses the existing integration as negotiating capital rather than discarding it. I will keep the option open to revisit switch_primary_vendor or add_second_source at the next review once utilization is healthier, but I will not bundle that into this cycle's single decision.
